edits.new:
Their $\eta A_{\rm rx}$ is 3–5× below the model's 0.81 cm² ($0.81/0.28=2.9$ and $0.81/0.16=5.1$), consistent with the lower PDE of 2013–2018 detectors.
- **Panasonic's photon count.** Its four sources give $4\times300\ {\rm W}\times10\ {\rm ns}=12\ \mu{\rm J}$ per pulse, which, spread evenly over $688\times384=2.64\times10^{5}$ pixels (illumination filling the camera's field), is $E_{\rm px}=45$ pJ per pixel. Eq. (55) solved for the count, with $\eta=1$ because the paper counts photons arriving at a pixel through the lens, before the PDE, gives $\bar n=\rho E_{\rm px}A_{\rm rx}/(\pi R^2E_{\rm ph})$. The aperture of the f/1.4 lens is $D=f/1.4$, and its focal length $f$ follows from the field across the 7.71 mm width of the array ($688\times11.2\ \mu{\rm m}$): $f=3.85\ {\rm mm}/\tan10^\circ=21.9$ mm for a 20° field and $3.85\ {\rm mm}/\tan5^\circ=44.0$ mm for 10°, i.e. $D=15.6$ and 31.5 mm. At 100 m on 10%, $\bar n=0.1\times4.54\times10^{-11}\ {\rm J}\times1.91\times10^{-4}\ {\rm m^2}/(\pi\times(100\ {\rm m})^2\times2.11\times10^{-19}\ {\rm J})=0.13$ for the 20° field, and 0.53 with the 31.5 mm lens ($A_{\rm rx}=7.77\times10^{-4}$ m²). The paper's Figure 2, for 1.2 kW, 10 ns, a 20° field and a 10% target, shows ≈1.2 photons at 100 m and crosses one near 110 m. It gives no aperture or losses for that curve, which lies 9× above the model's 0.13 for the same field [P, Hirose et al. 2018, §2 and Fig. 2; E].
